name: Tremella mushroom

card.summary: Snow fungus polysaccharide marketed as a hydrator; support is patents and reported claims, not trials.

quick.overview:
Tremella is an edible gelatinous fungus whose polysaccharide extracts are used in Asian skincare as moisturisers and brightening agents.

The sources found are encyclopedic descriptions and patents; no clinical trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Its polysaccharides are described as water-absorbing and water-holding, and a patent reports inhibition of melanin formation.
quick.risks: No skincare safety data were found; the fungus is a long-established food.

lead: Tremella fuciformis, known as snow fungus or silver ear, is an edible, gelatinous white fungus whose polysaccharide extracts are used in Asian skincare as moisturisers and for anti-wrinkle and brightening effects. People use tremella-based products, and eat the fungus in soups and desserts, for skin that looks hydrated and plump.[1]

Wikipedia reports that extracts appear in beauty products in China, Korea and Japan and are said to increase moisture retention in the skin, possibly reduce wrinkles and raise superoxide dismutase, an antioxidant enzyme; it presents these as reported claims.[1] A US patent describes a tremella polysaccharide for skin care with moisturising and melanin-formation-inhibiting effects.[2]

A human study of a snow mushroom hand gel in 20 volunteers found it moisturised the skin significantly better than placebo at all time points up to 180 minutes and was non-irritating.[3] A 2025 review summarises tremella polysaccharide research, mostly on immune, antioxidant and metabolic activities.[4]

angle.text: Tremella polysaccharide is used in creams and serums as a water-holding ingredient, with the aim of plumper, more hydrated-looking skin. Some products position it as a plant-based alternative to other humectants.

paras: The fungus forms white, frond-like fruit bodies up to about 7 cm across and grows as a parasitic yeast on other fungi on dead broadleaf wood. Berkeley described it in 1856 from Brazilian collections.[1] It has been cultivated in China since at least the 19th century, and a modern dual-culture method with its host fungus is used; estimated Chinese output in 1997 was 130,000 tonnes.[1]
Traditionally it is used in sweet soups and desserts such as the Cantonese dessert soup luk mei and, in traditional Chinese medicine, is valued for nourishing the lungs and increasing yin.[1]

In cosmetics, extracts are reported to retain moisture, reduce wrinkles and raise superoxide dismutase levels; Wikipedia presents these as reported claims.[1] A 2006 US patent describes a tremella polysaccharide for skin care with moisturizing and melanin-formation-inhibiting effects.[2] A 2008 patent describes use for intestinal disorders.[5]

A 2021 Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology study formulated an alcohol-based hand gel with 10 percent snow mushroom extract and tested it in 20 Thai volunteers. The gel moisturised the skin significantly better than placebo at all intervals through 180 minutes, caused no irritation and had antiseptic efficacy comparable with the placebo gel.[3]

A 2023 randomized trial of a fish roe, snow fungus and yeast supplement examined cognitive function rather than skin.[6] No studies found of tremella skincare on facial wrinkles or pigmentation. A 2025 review covers extraction, structure and bioactivities of tremella polysaccharides, including immunomodulatory, antioxidant, anti-hyperglycemic and anti-hyperlipidemia effects.[4]
